extracted.intended_audience: researchers, academics, and readers interested in research integrity and retractions (Retraction Watch readership)
extracted.subtask_description: News-style reporting of a specific journal article retraction due to data fabrication, summarizing the retraction notice, relevant facts (citations, funding, related thesis), and follow-up actions (contacting institution, commentary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Data fabrication (as stated in retraction notice)
rubrics_metrics.description: "This article is being retracted, in agreement with all authors, due to data fabrication. The first author of this paper, Sarah Michelle Norris, has acknowledged that she fabricated data on the effects of cyclopiazonic acid (CPA) ... in order to report a positive experimental outcome."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction notice gives a specific factual account: the actual experimental data showed CPA had no effect on muscle oxygen consumption but the author reported a progressive reduction peaking at a 50% reduction with 10 μM CPA. Use direct statements of what was fabricated (which assays/conditions and reported effects) when documenting misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction statement should specify authors' agreement and reason
rubrics_metrics.description: "This article is being retracted, in agreement with all authors, due to data fabrication."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notice explicitly states both the reason for retraction (data fabrication) and that the retraction is made "in agreement with all authors." When issuing a retraction, include clear cause and indicate authors' stance/consent where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration of co-authors' (non-)involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: "None of the co-authors participated in or had knowledge of the first author’s actions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction notices may (and in this case do) state whether co-authors were involved or aware. Such declarations inform disputes about responsibility; they should be explicit about who participated in the misconduct and who did not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check related works (theses, other papers) for compromise
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter notes: "It looks like Norris was doing similar work for her 2009 masters’ thesis... We wonder if that paper might also be compromised."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When fabrication is discovered in a published paper, related outputs (theses, closely related articles by the same author or group) should be reviewed for possible compromise. Reporters and institutions should flag and investigate connected works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notify and involve institutional oversight (supervisor, research integrity officer)
rubrics_metrics.description: The post: "We have attempted to reach her supervisor, A. Russell Tupling, but have yet to hear back. We also have a message out to Waterloo’s top research integrity officer and will update this post when we learn more."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists and concerned parties should contact supervisors and institutional research integrity officers; institutions are the appropriate bodies to investigate allegations and provide official responses. Document attempts and any institutional replies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document citation impact and funding when reporting retractions
rubrics_metrics.description: "The study has been cited six times ... and was funded by the Canadian government: This work was supported by Grant MOP-86618 from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research ..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports of retractions should record how often the work has been cited and disclose funding sources. This information helps assess downstream impact and potential obligations to funders or corrective notifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community scrutiny and questions about authorship responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Commentary observes and questions authorship practices: e.g. "If all these other people had nothing to do with it and no idea, then why were they co-authors?" and discussion of "courtesy authors" or committee oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public reporting of retractions often prompts debate about co-authorship norms, oversight, and responsibility. Such community commentary highlights expectations that co-authors should have meaningful involvement or verification, and raises systemic issues (e.g., courtesy authorship, inadequate data checking) to be addressed.
